chapter_theme: On the shore after the sea festival, Madhavi tunes the yazh and hands it to Kovalan, who sings the Kaveri as the Chola's wife whose chastity is not to sulk at his other loves, then a run of neithal songs in the voices of the shore girls and of the smitten man, calling the fisher girl moon, goddess and Death in disguise; the songs, chosen by him for pleasure, carry the hint of another love that Madhavi will answer and that ends their union.

cast.role: son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer and courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lives
the river Kaveri, addressed in the songs as the Chola's wife

silappathikaram:7:1-20.reading: On the seashore Madhavi takes up the yazh, adorned like a bride and free of faults in body, neck, pegs and strings, worships it, runs through the eight ways of handling the strings and tests by ear the eight ways of fingering, then holds it out to Kovalan asking what song he commands, and he begins to play songs of the Kaveri and of the shore groves to delight her.
silappathikaram:7:1-20.nuance: The unit is a catalogue of the lute-player's craft (two named lists of eight techniques, lines 5-8 and 12-15), and the instrument is dressed like a bride before the songs begin. The act that matters for the story is small: Madhavi hands the yazh to Kovalan (line 18), so the songs that follow are his choice, and the kaathai's close (line 289) will lay the parting on what the two sang over this yazh.
silappathikaram:7:1-20.event: Madhavi tunes the yazh and hands it to Kovalan, who begins to play songs of the Kaveri and the seashore for her.

silappathikaram:7:21-28.reading: Kovalan hails the Kaveri: though the Chola of the moon-white umbrella, wielding his just sceptre, unites with the Ganga, she does not sulk, and he says he knows that this not sulking, carp-eyed one, is the great chastity of a noble woman.
silappathikaram:7:21-28.nuance: The river is the Chola's wife and the Ganga the other woman his northern conquest has taken; the praise of the king is turned into a picture of marriage in which the wife's virtue is to bear his other union without sulking. Sung by a married man to the courtesan he lives with, while his own wife waits at home, the stanza touches all three; the kaathai shows Madhavi reading a hidden meaning in these songs (lines 144-148).

claims.claim: a wife who does not sulk when her husband unites with another shows the great chastity of a noble woman

silappathikaram:7:29-36.reading: The second stanza repeats the praise with the Kanni, the southern maiden river, in place of the Ganga: though the Chola of the unbending sceptre unites with her, the Kaveri does not sulk, and that is a woman's lasting great chastity.
silappathikaram:7:29-36.nuance: With the Ganga in the north and the Kanni in the south, the two stanzas give the king a rival bride at each end of the land, so the Kaveri's patience covers the whole reach of his conquest. வளையாச் செங்கோல் (line 30) makes the uniting with another a mark of his just rule, not a fault.

claims.claim: a wife who does not sulk when her husband unites with another keeps a woman's lasting chastity

silappathikaram:7:37-44.reading: The third stanza hears the Kaveri walking amid the shouts of ploughmen, the roar of sluices and breaking water and the cries of the festival crowds, and calls all that she has walked through, loud with the Mazhavar warriors, the very wealth of the Chola Valavan.
silappathikaram:7:37-44.nuance: After two stanzas of the river as wife, this one makes her the source of the king's prosperity, so the couple of river and king is both a marriage and an economy. The sense of வாய்காவா (line 42), said of the Mazhavar, is not settled.

silappathikaram:7:45-52.reading: In the voice of the shore girls, the singer asks the lover how they, simple as they are, could have known that the man who showed the sea god again and again before the dark-eyed girl and swore a hard oath would break it and prove without virtue, and names their town as Puhar, where the water lily opens its buds taking white conches and pearls for the moon and stars.
silappathikaram:7:45-52.nuance: This is the akam friend's charge against a man who has broken his oath, sung as a set piece; the closing refrain (புகாரே எம்மூர்) turns each stanza into a boast of the city. The lily that mistakes conches and pearls for the moon and stars is the same mistake the girl made in trusting appearances.

claims.claim: those who break a hard-sworn oath are without virtue

silappathikaram:7:53-60.reading: The girls ask how they could have known that the man who became their lover, following them in the backwater grove with gifts, would stand like a stranger while they plead, and name Puhar as their town, where the bee swings unable to tell women's eyes from the blue lilies that bloom paired with the moon's reflection in the water.
silappathikaram:7:53-60.nuance: The lover's change is set as a turn from காதலர் to ஏதிலர் (lines 53, 55): the same man, first the one who followed with gifts, now the one they must beg. The bee that cannot choose between eye and flower mirrors the lover's wavering.

silappathikaram:7:61-68.reading: The third stanza pictures a conch, battered by old waves, ploughing through and spoiling a girl's sand-play on the striped beach, and the girl, distressed, flinging her kuvalai garland at it with soft fingers so that the flowers seem to glance sidelong, and in this Puhar those who pass cannot leave.
silappathikaram:7:61-68.nuance: Only here, of the three stanzas, there is no accusation; the girl's small anger is enough to hold the passers-by, and the garland's flowers, like eyes, do the looking. The spoiled sand-play is a stock neithal sign of the lover's first coming.

silappathikaram:7:69-75.reading: The singer sets the scene of the shore grove, where the trace the conch ploughed in the sand is hidden under the fine pollen of punnai flowers, and wonders whether the incurable sickness that her moon-bright face and carp eyes have given will be cured only by her soft breasts with their golden spots.
silappathikaram:7:69-75.nuance: The trace in the sand covered by falling pollen may stand for a union that leaves no sign, but the song does not say so. The syntax of தீர்க்கும் போலும் (line 75) leaves open whether the singer hopes or only supposes that the one who caused the sickness can cure it.

silappathikaram:7:76-82.reading: In the man's voice, the singer says that he did not know that in the fragrant shore grove there dwelt a goddess who, with driving birds from drying fish as her pretext, walks holding fresh njaazhal flowers swarmed by bees, and that had he known he would not have come.
silappathikaram:7:76-82.nuance: The refrain அறியேன் அறிவேனேல் அடையேன் (lines 81-82) makes first sight a danger the man would have avoided if warned; the girl's work, guarding the drying fish, is called a mere pretext for a goddess's presence.

silappathikaram:7:83-89.reading: The second stanza says that in the fishers' quarter, where nets dry before the houses, another being, a cruel Death with long eyes like killing spears, has taken a form of its choosing and lives in the cool shore grove, holding flowers, on the pretext of drying fish for sale; he did not know, and had he known he would not have come.
silappathikaram:7:83-89.nuance: வேண்டுஉருவம் கொண்டு (lines 85-86) makes the girl a disguise: Death has chosen to take a woman's shape, which is stronger than calling her eyes deadly.

silappathikaram:7:90-93.reading: The singer bids his hearers look: the face on which carp, bow, cloud and Kama's work have been drawn is the moon, which, fearing the serpent in the beautiful sky, has come to live in the boatmen's little village.
silappathikaram:7:90-93.nuance: The features are listed as things painted (எழுதி) on the face, eyes as carp, brows as bow, hair as cloud, and the moon is given a motive for coming down to earth: fear of the eclipse serpent.

silappathikaram:7:94-97.reading: He bids them look again: the stained spear-like eyes that run to either side as her bangles ring are fierce Death, which in the sea-dwellers' little village has become a girl of soft and innocent grace.
silappathikaram:7:94-97.nuance: The stanza joins the deadliest name to the gentlest: கடுங்கூற்றம் becomes மடம்கெழுமென் சாயல் மகள் (lines 96-97), so innocence is the form the killing takes.

silappathikaram:7:98-101.reading: He bids them look a third time: the goddess who brings anguish to those who see her driving birds from the white drying fish has taken the form of a woman with five-braided hair in the cool shore grove where the adumbu creeper grows.
silappathikaram:7:98-101.nuance: The three nilaivari stanzas name her moon, Death and goddess in turn, each come down to the fishing village in human form. The force of அலவநோய் (line 99) is not certain.

silappathikaram:7:102-105.reading: The singer lists the grove's fragrant flowers, the fresh-scented sand, her flawless words, her young breasts, her moon-like face, her curved brows and her waist too fine to paint, and says these are what brought him distress.
silappathikaram:7:102-105.nuance: Each line runs two vocatives, and the place and the woman are mixed in one list, so the grove itself is among the causes of the sickness.

silappathikaram:7:106-109.reading: The second stanza lists the ford where waves spread, the broad sand, the fragrant flowers, the thick grove, her braided hair, her moon-like face and her paired carp eyes as what brought him distress.

silappathikaram:7:110-113.reading: The third stanza lists the ford where conches grow, the fragrant grove, the opening flowers, the place where she walks alone, her budding smile, her moon-like face and the young girl's breasts as what brought him distress.
silappathikaram:7:110-113.nuance: தனிஅவள் திரிஇடமே (line 111) adds the one hint of a meeting: the place where she wanders alone.

silappathikaram:7:114-117.reading: The singer tells the fisher girl that her elders live by going into the sea and taking lives, and she too lives by going into bodies and taking lives, and warns her that under the weight of breasts no strength can contain, her waist, sinking in distress, will be lost.
silappathikaram:7:114-117.nuance: The fishers' trade of killing is taken as the plain fact of the coast and turned into a compliment: the daughter inherits the family work, killing lives, with her body as the net. The warning about the waist is the usual hyperbole of praise.

silappathikaram:7:118-121.reading: The second stanza says her father kills lives with a crooked-meshed net and she kills lives with the net of her long eyes, and warns her that with breasts bearing strands of pearls her waist, swaying like lightning in rain, will snap.
silappathikaram:7:118-121.nuance: The pun is in வலை: கொடுங்கண் வலை, the net of crooked mesh, against நெடுங்கண் வலை, the net of long eyes (lines 118-119).

links.note: Madhavi hands Kovalan the yazh and he chooses the songs; at the kaathai's close the narrator says his old deed came to fruit over the yazh music and he left her.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the narrator placing the first turn of the story's karma not in a crime or a curse but in a lute passed between lovers at play, so the moral of the patikam that past deeds come to fruit begins with a song chosen for pleasure.

links.note: Kovalan's Kaveri proves her chastity by not sulking when the Chola unites with the Ganga; Madhavi's Kaveri walks as she does because her husband's sceptre never bends.
links.teaches: Sung back over the same river, the two stanzas put the burden of fidelity on opposite partners: Kovalan asks the wife to bear the husband's other union, Madhavi makes the river's grace the sign of a husband who keeps straight, so the exchange is a quarrel about who owes faithfulness.

links.note: The song praises a wife who does not sulk at her husband's other love; Madhavi hears in Kovalan's songs a hidden intent and takes up the yazh in a sulk disguised as pleasure.
links.teaches: The song's ideal of the wife who never sulks is answered at once by the courtesan's sulking, so the kaathai shows the praise of patient chastity working as a provocation on the one woman who is not his wife.

links.note: In the Ainkurunuru the wife begins to push away her husband's chest, broad as the Kaveri's full flood, in sulking; in the vari the Kaveri herself is the wife who never sulks at the Chola's other unions.
links.teaches: The Sangam marutham gives the Kaveri's flood to the straying husband and lets the wife sulk at it, while the epic song makes the river the wife and her not sulking the highest chastity, so the same river image moves from licensing the wife's oodal to forbidding it.

gains.a: the stanza's demand for a wife without oodal stands out against the older convention in which the wronged wife's sulking was expected and even loved
gains.b: the quatrain's playful river-chest gains a later reading in which the river is no longer the husband's breadth but the wife's patience

links.note: The couplet makes sulking love's salt, good in right measure and spoiling only when overdone; the stanza calls not sulking at all, even at the husband's other union, a woman's great chastity.
links.teaches: Where the Kural sets a measure for oodal, the epic song sets it at nothing and names that karpu, so together they show the measure of sulking turning from a matter of love's taste into a test of a wife's virtue.

gains.a: the stanza's praise gains a standard to be measured against: by the couplet it asks for no salt at all
gains.b: the couplet's measure gains its limit case, a song that would remove sulking entirely from a wife's part

links.note: The Akananuru friend asks the lord of the shore whether the oath he swore when his chariot crushed the girls' sand dolls was false too, with the sea as witness; the vari asks how simple girls could know that the man who swore by the sea god would break it.
links.teaches: The pair shows the epic lifting the neithal friend's charge, an oath with the sea as witness and the girls' sand-play spoiled, out of the courtship plot where it pressed for marriage and into a sung entertainment, where the charge of broken faith is performed by the man who will himself walk out at the song's end.

gains.a: the stanza gains its source situation: the sea-oath and the spoiled sand-play were a friend's demand for marriage before they were a song for a courtesan
gains.b: the Akananuru poem gains evidence that its situation had become a fixed piece of Puhar song, recognisable enough to be sung by a merchant at the shore festival

links.note: Kovalan sings the girls' blame of a man who swore by the sea god and broke his word; when Madhavi answers in song, he decides she is the deceiver and leaves her.
links.teaches: The singer who voiced the charge against the oath-breaking man ends the kaathai by abandoning his woman and calling her the one full of lying tricks, so the story turns the song's accusation back on the one who sang it.

links.note: The couplet says this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; the vari asks whether the sickness her face and eyes gave can be cured only by her breasts.
links.teaches: The song splits the couplet's paradox across the body, the eyes and face causing the sickness and the breasts curing it, which shows how a later lyric turned the Kural's single riddle into a scene of parts.

gains.a: the stanza's closing guess gains a known paradox behind it, that the beloved breaks the rule of medicine by being both cause and cure
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete setting and a division of roles within the woman's body that it leaves unstated

links.note: The couplet's man says he never knew Death before and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes; the vari's man says he did not know Death lived in the shore grove, and had he known he would not have come.
links.teaches: Both men learn Death in a woman's eyes, but the Kural's man ends in recognition while the song's ends in the wish never to have come, so the pair separates knowing love's danger from wanting to have avoided it.

gains.a: the stanza's refrain gains a contrast that shows its regret as a choice: the couplet's speaker accepts what he now knows
gains.b: the couplet's moment of discovery gains a sequel in which the knowledge comes too late to act on

links.note: The couplet asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe and finds all three in it; the vari asks whether her eyes are fierce Death and answers that Death has become an innocent girl.
links.teaches: Where the Kural holds Death and the doe's innocence side by side in one look, the song makes one the form of the other, so the innocent girl is Death in disguise, a step from mixture to transformation.

gains.a: the stanza's turn gains a reference point: it resolves into one being what the couplet leaves as three natures
gains.b: the couplet's list gains a storytelling form in which its opposites are joined by the god of death taking a girl's shape

links.note: The Thinaimalai man says the girl guarding drying fish turns weapon-eyes on him and it is he, not the fish, she guards; the vari says the goddess who afflicts those who see her driving birds from drying fish has taken a woman's form.
links.teaches: The same fish-guarding girl is a wry reversal of guarding in the akam verse and a goddess in disguise in the epic song, so the pair shows the neithal scene moving from the lover's joke to a performance piece of supernatural praise.

gains.a: the stanza gains its plain source scene, in which the girl's task and the man's capture are human and comic
gains.b: the akam verse gains a later form in which its girl is lifted into an anangu, showing how the stock scene was elevated in courtly song

links.note: The couplet calls those whose work is killing base in the eyes of the discerning; the vari tells the fisher girl that her elders live by killing lives in the sea and she by killing lives in men's bodies.
links.teaches: The ethics book brands killing for a living as base, while the coastal song takes the fishers' killing as the plain inheritance of a family and makes it a compliment, so the pair shows a whole people's livelihood that the Kural's judgment would fall on and that the poetry of the shore never questions.

gains.a: the stanza's easy wit about killing gains an ethical weight it does not register: by the Kural's standard the father's trade is base work
gains.b: the couplet's judgment gains a concrete people it would condemn, the fishing families the epic sings with admiration

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
